passage:
"It's impossible!" Tarun glared at the triangle in his notebook. "Twenty minutes and it still doesn't work!"
"Then close the book," said his mother Neelam. "Go and play."
"But it's homework."
"It will be here when you come back."
Tarun kicked the ball around the courtyard for half an hour. When he came in, red-faced and thirsty, he picked up his pencil and looked at the figure again.
"Oh!" he said. "I wrote AB where it should be BC. I mislabelled the sides!"
He fixed them and finished the problem in five minutes.
"Ma, it was that easy."

qa.q: How long did Tarun stare at the triangle before he stopped?
qa.a: He had worked on it for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he said "It's impossible!"?
qa.a: He was frustrated and stuck. He glared at the notebook and thought twenty minutes should have been enough.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Tarun use the next time he is stuck, and why?
qa.a: He could check the labels on his figure and read the question again before quitting. Small slips in labelling can hide behind a problem that seems impossible.

qa.q: How does Neelam see Tarun's stuck problem?
qa.a: Neelam sees a boy who is tired and wound up, so she sends him to play, trusting the problem will look different afterwards. 😊

grounding: A boy stares at a geometry problem for twenty minutes, goes to play, and on returning sees he mislabelled the sides and finishes it in five.

passage: Last week a triangle problem nearly beat me. Find the missing angle, with two sides marked equal. I stared at it for twenty minutes. My answer kept coming out as 140°, which can't be right in a triangle that already has a 70° angle. My head felt like wet cotton. Then the boys downstairs shouted for football, and I just went. I played for half an hour. When I came back, sweaty, and looked at the drawing again, I saw it at once: I had marked the wrong two sides as equal. I fixed the labels and finished in five minutes. Minakshi Aunty, passing the door, said, 'Pema beta, see? Your brain needed air.'

qa.q: How long did Pema play football?
How did Pema feel after twenty minutes of staring?
qa.a: Pema felt foggy and frustrated, with a head 'like wet cotton' and an answer that couldn't be right.

qa.q: What could Pema try next time he's stuck like this?
qa.a: Take a short break sooner, then check the labels first; the rest let him see the mistake he'd been staring past.

qa.q: How does Minakshi Aunty see what happened?
qa.a: Minakshi Aunty thinks his brain simply needed air, so she sees the break as part of solving it, not time wasted.

grounding: Shows a boy who stares at a geometry problem for twenty minutes, goes out to play, and on returning spots his mislabelled sides and finishes quickly.

passage: Tuition note, Friday. Rafiq sat over one geometry question for twenty minutes today, the one with the parallelogram. He kept writing and rubbing out, and his perimeter kept coming out too small. Then he pushed back his chair and asked if he could throw the ball with Pranav in the yard for ten minutes. I said yes. When he came back and looked at his drawing, he said, 'Oh! I called this side 6 and it's the 9 one.' He relabelled the sides and finished in five minutes. I'm going to suggest short breaks to the whole group when someone is stuck this long.

qa.q: Which shape was in Rafiq's geometry question?
What might Rafiq have felt when he said 'Oh!'?
qa.a: He probably felt surprised and relieved, suddenly seeing he had swapped the 6 and 9 sides.

qa.q: What does this suggest for other students who get stuck?
qa.a: A short break after a long stuck spell can help them return and spot mistakes, like a wrong label, that staring missed.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Rafiq's break?
qa.a: The note-writer saw it work so well that short breaks will now be suggested to the whole group.

grounding: Illustrates a boy leaving a puzzling geometry problem for a break outside and, on returning, seeing he mislabelled the sides and finishing quickly.
